The  significance  of  sympathy  for  ethical 
theory  is  connected  with  the  important 
practical  distinction  between  egoistic  and 
altruistic  interests.  When  moral  conduct  i.s 
identified  with  rational  conduct,  and  the  life 
of  reason  is  separated  from  the  emotional 
life  (as  by  the  Stoics  and  by  Kant),  this  dis 
tinction  between  egoism  and  altruism  is  not 
regarded  as  fundamental,  and  sympathy  is 
not  held  either  to  constitute  or  to  lead  to 
morality.  Hut  wherever  the  distinction  of 
egoistic  and  altruistic  conduct  has  become 
prominent  (as  in  the  English  successors  and 
opponents  of  Hobbes),  the  part  played  by 
sympathy  both  in  determining  conduct  and 
in  evaluating  it  has  come  to  be  looked  upon 
as  of  primary  importance.  The  classical  con 
dition  for  the  ethical  value  of  sympathy  is 
found  in  the  Moral  Sentiments  of  Adam  Smith. 
According  to  him  the  effort  to  sympathize 
produces  both  the  '  amiable  '  and  the  '  noble  ' 
virtues  of  character;  and  the  sympathy  of
